findings.quote: A recent open-label, single-arm study using monetary CM evaluated the cognitive and clinical effects of 28 days of cannabis abstinence among individuals with co-morbid MDD and CUD.
findings.text: In one study, 28 days of monetary contingency management led people who use cannabis to achieve abstinence and improve cognitive and depressive symptoms.

findings.quote: Coinciding with abstinence and reductions in use, significant improvements in select cognitive domains, including visual search speed, visual sustained attention and response inhibition, and VSWM were found.
findings.text: In the same study, abstinence and reduced use were associated with significant improvements in visual search speed, sustained attention, response inhibition, and visual working memory.

findings.quote: Concerning clinical outcomes associated with cannabis abstinence, improvements in depressive symptomology and anhedonia were observed; cannabis abstinence led to non-significant improvements in anxiety symptomology.
findings.text: In that study, cannabis abstinence led to improvements in depressive symptoms and anhedonia, but not in anxiety symptoms.

limits.quote: First, our sample size was small due to the limited number of studies exploring the efficacy of CM for CUD in psychiatric populations.
limits.text: The review’s findings are limited by the small sample size of the included studies.
